items.prompt: What is a bounded context?
choices: A boundary inside which terms are consistent and one group owns the data
A server that runs exactly one module
items.explanation: It is defined by consistent meaning and clear ownership inside its line.
items.reference:
Bounded context
🏷️ A term means one consistent thing inside
👥 One group owns the data
🚧 Code changes without permission from the other side

Why: a bounded context is defined by meaning and ownership, not by deployment; same word may legitimately mean different things in two contexts.
items.reflection: A word like 'account' means one thing to a bank teller and another to a security engineer. Where else have you seen one word carry different meanings in different groups, and how did people avoid confusion?

items.prompt: Coupling measures...
choices: How many lines of code it has
How much a group depends on things outside it
items.explanation: Coupling is dependence across the line.
items.reference:
Two numbers
🔗 Coupling — dependence on things outside the group (want low)
🧲 Cohesion — dependence inside the group (want high)
✂️ Good boundary: low out, high in

Why: high coupling out means a network line through the group turns local calls and transactions into distributed ones.
items.reflection: A kitchen where every chef constantly borrows tools from other stations is hard to split into two kitchens. Where else have you seen a group that looked separable but leaned heavily on neighbors?

items.prompt: In the call graph, what does a node represent?
items.explanation: Each module becomes a node.
items.reference:
Reading the graph
⚪ Node = module
➡️ Solid edge = calls, weighted per day
⋯ Dotted edge = shared table (stronger)

Why: a call can be replaced by an API, but a shared table cannot be separated until one side moves its data.
items.reflection: A road map shows highways and tiny paths differently because they constrain you differently. What other maps have you used where one kind of connection mattered much more than another?
